title: UI & Visual Design
description: Apply hierarchy, typography, spacing systems, colour and WCAG contrast to interface designs.

questions.prompt: A cart page shows three buttons side by side: 'Continue to payment', 'Save cart for later' and 'Apply coupon'. All three are the same size and the same solid blue, and users hesitate before proceeding. Which change establishes a clear visual hierarchy?

options.text: Make all three buttons larger so their labels are easier to read
Give each button a different bright colour so all three are distinct
Keep 'Continue to payment' as the solid filled button and restyle the other two as outlined or text buttons
Add an icon to each button while keeping the identical blue styling

questions.explanation: Hierarchy comes from contrast in visual weight: one dominant primary action and visually quieter secondary actions. Giving all three buttons different bright colours keeps them equally loud, so nothing tells the user which action matters most.

questions.prompt: In a sign-up form, each label sits 16px above its input and also 16px below the previous input. Testers sometimes type into the wrong field. Which spacing change applies the Gestalt principle of proximity?

options.text: Cut label-to-input space to about 6px and widen gaps between fields to about 28px
Increase every gap equally to 32px so the whole form feels less cramped
Place each label to the right of its input instead of above it
Keep the current spacing but add a 1px divider line under every label

questions.explanation: Proximity means elements that are closer together read as a group, so the space inside a label-input pair should be clearly smaller than the space between pairs. Raising every gap to 32px keeps the spacing uniform, so labels are still equally close to the field above and the field below.

questions.prompt: A blog template renders 18px body text in a column that spans a 1440px-wide desktop viewport, giving roughly 150 characters per line. Readers say they lose their place moving to the next line. Which CSS change addresses this?

options.text: font-size: 24px; on body paragraphs
text-align: justify; on body paragraphs
letter-spacing: 0.1em; on body paragraphs
max-width: 65ch; on the article text column

questions.explanation: Comfortable reading needs lines of roughly 45-75 characters (Bringhurst; Baymard suggests 50-75), and limiting the column to about 65ch does this directly. Bigger text cuts the count somewhat, but lines would still run past 100 characters.

questions.prompt: A form shows invalid fields only by changing the input border from grey to red. Which change makes sure users who can't tell red from grey still know which field has an error?

options.text: Use a brighter, more saturated red for the error border
Add an error icon and a text message next to the field describing the problem
Change the error colour from red to orange, which is easier to see
Tint the field background light pink as well as making the border red

questions.explanation: Colour should never be the only way to show meaning (WCAG 2.2 SC 1.4.1 Use of Color), so the error needs a non-colour cue such as an icon plus text. A pink background is still a colour-only cue, so it doesn't help someone who can't perceive the colour difference.

questions.prompt: True or false: Under WCAG 2.2 Level AA, a 16px bold button label counts as 'large text', so it only needs a 3:1 contrast ratio against its background.
questions.explanation: WCAG defines large text as at least 18pt (24px) regular or 14pt (about 18.66px) bold. A 16px bold label is normal-size text, so it needs 4.5:1 under SC 1.4.3.

questions.prompt: A design review lists the colour pairs below with their measured contrast ratios. Which element fails WCAG 2.2 Level AA contrast requirements?

code.source:
Element                    Size / weight  Fg       Bg       Ratio
Body text                  16px regular   #6B7280  #FFFFFF  4.83:1
Primary button label       16px bold      #FFFFFF  #16A34A  3.30:1
Page heading               24px regular   #808080  #FFFFFF  3.95:1
Input border (sole edge)   1px solid      #949494  #FFFFFF  3.03:1

options.text: The body text
The primary button label
The page heading
The text input border

questions.explanation: A 16px bold label is not large text, so it needs 4.5:1 (SC 1.4.3), and 3.30:1 falls short. The 24px heading counts as large text and only needs 3:1, and the input border is a UI component that needs 3:1 under SC 1.4.11, so both pass.

questions.prompt: A design system uses a 4px-based spacing scale exposed as CSS custom properties, and every margin, padding and gap value in component CSS must use one of these tokens. Which line breaks that rule?
questions.explanation: Line 14 hard-codes 13px, which isn't a token and isn't even on the 4px scale, so spacing will drift from the system. border-radius on line 8 isn't a margin, padding or gap value, so the spacing rule doesn't apply to it.

questions.prompt: A type scale uses a 16px base and a ratio of 1.25 (Major Third). H4 is one step above the base, H3 is two steps above, and H2 is three steps above. What size is H2?

options.text: 28px
25px

questions.explanation: Each step multiplies by the ratio: 16 x 1.25^3 = 31.25px. 28px is what you get by adding 4px per step (a linear scale), and 25px is only two steps up, which is H3.

questions.prompt: A team builds a dark theme by inverting its light theme: page background #000000, cards #000000, and the same drop shadows as in light mode. Users say the cards blend into the page. Which approach follows established dark-theme guidance such as Material Design?

options.text: Use a dark grey base such as #121212 and make higher-elevation surfaces progressively lighter
Increase drop-shadow opacity to 100% black so the cards separate from the page
Add a pure white 2px border around every card to define its edges
Fill the cards with a saturated brand colour so they stand out from the page

questions.explanation: Shadows barely show against near-black, so Material Design's dark theme uses a dark grey base and shows elevation by making surfaces lighter (or more tinted) as they rise. Darker shadows can't separate a black card from a black page.

questions.prompt: A UI audit finds these text colours in production CSS. What is the most maintainable fix?

options.text: Keep every value but document each one, with usage notes, in the style guide
Replace all nine values with #333333 so that all text uses one colour
Define a few semantic tokens (e.g. text-primary, text-secondary), map each to a checked value, and replace raw hex codes
Convert each hex code to its rgb() equivalent so the values are easier to compare

questions.explanation: Semantic tokens consolidate near-duplicates into a small, intentional palette that can be changed in one place, and each value can be checked for contrast (for example #777777 on white is only 4.48:1). Collapsing everything to one colour removes the useful primary/secondary text hierarchy.

questions.prompt: Under WCAG 2.2 SC 1.4.11 Non-text Contrast (Level AA), which of these must have at least a 3:1 contrast ratio against adjacent colours? Select all that apply.

options.text: The border of a text input when that border is the only visual indication of the field
The magnifying-glass icon inside an icon-only search button
The outline of a disabled Submit button
A purely decorative background illustration on a landing page
The data lines in a line chart that users need in order to read the trend

questions.explanation: SC 1.4.11 covers the visual information needed to identify UI components and their states (input boundaries, meaningful icons) and graphics needed to understand content (chart lines). Inactive (disabled) components and purely decorative graphics are explicitly exempt.

questions.prompt: In a circular play button, the triangle icon is centred mathematically by its bounding box, yet reviewers say it looks shifted to the left. What is the correct fix?

options.text: Leave it, since mathematical centring is correct and viewers will adjust
Enlarge the triangle until its corners touch the edge of the circle
Add equal padding on all four sides of the triangle's bounding box
Nudge the triangle slightly right so its visual mass, not its bounding box, sits in the centre

questions.explanation: Most of a triangle's visual weight sits near its flat left side, so a box-centred triangle looks off-centre, and designers correct this with optical alignment. Equal padding is just another way of centring the bounding box, which is what causes the problem.

questions.prompt: The brand team wants blue #3B82F6 used everywhere on a white background. Given the measurements and usages below, which plan meets WCAG 2.2 AA while keeping the most brand blue?

code.source:
#3B82F6 on #FFFFFF = 3.68:1
#2563EB on #FFFFFF = 5.17:1

Planned uses of blue:
- inline links (underlined) in 16px regular body text
- 32px regular marketing headings
- 2px focus rings around controls
- icons in icon-only buttons

options.text: Use #2563EB for the 16px links; keep #3B82F6 for the headings, focus rings and icons, which need 3:1
Keep #3B82F6 for the links but make them bold, since bold text only needs 3:1
Keep #3B82F6 for the links, since underlined links are exempt from text contrast
Use #2563EB for all four uses, since anything below 4.5:1 fails AA

questions.explanation: 16px regular text needs 4.5:1 (SC 1.4.3), so the links need the darker shade. The 32px headings are large text and the focus rings and icons are non-text, so 3:1 is enough (SC 1.4.3/1.4.11) and 3.68:1 passes. Bolding 16px text doesn't make it large text, and an underline satisfies SC 1.4.1 Use of Color but doesn't exempt link text from SC 1.4.3 contrast.

questions.prompt: A marketing site sizes its headings with the rule below so they scale with the viewport. An accessibility review flags it. What is the problem, and what is the fix?

options.text: vw units are not supported in mobile browsers; switch to a fixed px value such as 48px
The heading becomes too large on phones; add a media query that sets it to 16px
vw-only sizes don't grow with browser zoom or the user's default font size; mix in rem, e.g. clamp(2rem, 1.5rem + 2vw, 4rem)
WCAG 1.4.4 requires every font size to be set in em; rem and vw both fail

questions.explanation: Zooming shrinks the CSS viewport, so text sized only in vw stays the same physical size and can fail SC 1.4.4 Resize Text. A rem component makes headings respond to zoom and user font settings. WCAG doesn't mandate any unit; it requires text that can resize to 200%.

questions.prompt: A team generated status colours by fixing HSL lightness at 50%, expecting equal contrast on white. The results are below. Why did this happen, and what is the better approach?

code.source:
warning  hsl(60 100% 50%)  = #FFFF00  -> 1.07:1 on white
success  hsl(120 100% 50%) = #00FF00  -> 1.37:1 on white
info     hsl(240 100% 50%) = #0000FF  -> 8.59:1 on white

options.text: The ratios were miscalculated, because equal HSL lightness always gives equal WCAG contrast
HSL lightness isn't perceptually uniform, so build scales in a perceptual space like OKLCH and check each contrast
100% saturation inflates contrast; setting every colour to 50% saturation will equalise it
WCAG contrast is based on the red channel only, so the scales should be defined in RGB

questions.explanation: WCAG relative luminance weights green and red far more heavily than blue, and HSL lightness ignores this, so same-L yellow and blue differ hugely in luminance. Perceptual spaces like OKLCH track perceived lightness much better, though contrast should still be checked. Lowering saturation alone doesn't fix the hue-dependent luminance gap.
